rows: UKHSA operates Heat-Health Alerts in partnership with the Met Office.
Alerts are issued when forecast heat could cause health impacts in England.
The core Heat-Health Alert season runs from 1 June to 30 September.
Extraordinary alerts can be issued outside the core season where impacts are expected.
The system uses green preparedness and yellow, amber and red response levels.
Yellow alerts can indicate risks concentrated among vulnerable groups or uncertainty about more significant impacts.
Amber alerts indicate wider impacts and may require a coordinated response.
Red alerts indicate a significant risk to life, including among healthy people.
Heat-health alerts are regional, dynamic forecast-based signals and not measurements inside a specific building.
Operational use requires checking the current dashboard, region, alert period and locally applicable response plan.
Norovirus commonly causes sudden vomiting and diarrhoea.
Norovirus spreads readily in settings involving close contact.
Symptoms commonly develop around 12 to 48 hours after infection.
Most people recover within about 2 to 3 days.
People should stay away from work or school until 48 hours after symptoms have stopped.
People should avoid preparing food for others until 48 hours after symptoms have stopped.
Handwashing with soap and warm water is important for reducing spread.
Alcohol-based hand sanitiser does not reliably kill norovirus.
General norovirus guidance does not establish an outbreak or contamination at a particular premises.
Case or outbreak conclusions require current authorised clinical, laboratory or health-protection evidence.
UKHSA provides home-isolation guidance for people diagnosed with mpox.
The guidance also covers people awaiting a test result who have been advised to self-isolate.
Measures are intended to reduce transmission to other household members.
Separate cleaning guidance applies during isolation.
Additional cleaning guidance applies when isolation ends.
Contacts of cases are covered by separate public-health guidance.
Vaccination and background information are provided through separate official resources.
Hospital de-isolation and discharge decisions should be made case by case.
General mpox guidance does not demonstrate infection at a particular home or premises.
Isolation, contact and cleaning actions depend on current clinical and public-health instructions for the individual case.
Rabies is a viral infection of the nervous system that is usually fatal after symptoms develop.
Human rabies cases are extremely rare in the UK and are usually acquired abroad.
Rabies is commonly transmitted through bites or scratches from infected mammals.
Potentially exposed wounds should be washed thoroughly with soap and water.
People exposed in a rabies-risk country should seek medical assessment without delay.
Assessment and post-exposure treatment should not wait until return to the UK.
Prompt post-exposure vaccination, and immunoglobulin where indicated, can prevent disease.
UKHSA guidance supports risk assessment and management of potential exposures.
Country risk, animal species, exposure type and treatment history materially affect the assessment.
A location or travel destination alone cannot establish exposure; individual contact and treatment evidence is required.
